nodes.label: The Achaemenid Empire
nodes.full: Under Cyrus and Cambyses the Persian Empire absorbed the Oman peninsula as the satrapal land of Maka — the first time the peninsula's oases had a formal place in a state stretching from the Aegean to the Indus.
nodes.src: background — Maka in the Bisitun inscription; Herodotus 3.93.

nodes.label: The Assyrians and the north
nodes.full: The Neo-Assyrian and then Neo-Babylonian world to the north-west: the powers whose incense demand and long-distance trade the newly camel-connected peninsula was now plugged into.
nodes.src: background — the Iron Age III South Arabian incense trade (Magee 2014).

nodes.label: South Arabia and the incense road
nodes.full: The kingdoms of the Yemeni highlands and the Hadhramaut, and the frankincense route the domesticated camel let Magan's oases finally reach overland.
nodes.src: background — the caravan networks of first-millennium Arabia.

nodes.label: The Iron Age settlement boom
nodes.full: With the falaj bringing water to new land, the Iron Age saw the densest settlement the peninsula had yet known — planned villages with columned halls, fortified hilltops and metal workshops. This is the society the Assyrians and then the Persians encountered.
nodes.src: P. Magee, 'The Iron Age of southeastern Arabia' and the Muweilah excavations; Rumeilah (Boucharlat & Lombard); al-Thuqaibah / Wadi al-Qawr (Spanish mission).

nodes.label: The peninsula as the satrapy of Maka
nodes.full: Persian royal inscriptions and the Persepolis reliefs list 'Maka' — the Oman peninsula — among the lands of the empire, its people shown bringing a dromedary and folded garments to the king. Magan ends this folio as the seaward corner of the Achaemenid world.
nodes.src: Maciya / Maka in the Bisitun, Naqsh-e Rostam and Persepolis (DPe, DNa) lists; the Maciya delegation on the Apadana reliefs. Herodotus 3.93, 7.68 ('Mykoi').

nodes.label: The burning of the columned hall at Muweilah
nodes.full: Muweilah's large pillared building — a communal or administrative hall stocked with grain, bronze and incense burners — was destroyed by fire around 600 BC and not rebuilt. The cause is unknown, but it marks a violent break in the Iron Age settlement.
nodes.src: P. Magee et al., Muweilah excavation reports (Area A columned building destruction horizon).

nodes.label: Maka contingents in the Persian army
nodes.full: Herodotus lists the 'Mykoi' — men of Maka — among the peoples marching with Xerxes, equipped with bows and short spears. Magan's Iron Age communities now owed military service to a distant emperor.
nodes.src: Herodotus 7.68. The identification of the Mykoi with the Oman peninsula's Maka is standard (Potts 1990, vol. 2).

nodes.label: The falaj — a communal institution for shared water
nodes.full: Running water from an aquifer to the fields through a graded tunnel only works if its upkeep, and the division of its flow, are governed by rule. The Iron Age falaj brought with it a system of timed water shares that still governs Omani and Emirati oases.
nodes.src: W. Al-Tikriti, 'The south-east Arabian origin of the falaj system', PSAS 32 (2002); the later codified water-rota (dawran) recorded for the Aflaj of Oman (UNESCO, 2006).

nodes.label: Iron Age columned halls as redistribution centres
nodes.full: Large buildings with rows of stone or wooden columns, holding stores of grain, metal and incense equipment, stand at the centre of several Iron Age villages. They look like places where a community's surplus was gathered, held and shared out.
nodes.src: Magee on the Muweilah columned buildings; Boucharlat & Lombard on Rumeilah Building II.

nodes.label: Maka under Achaemenid tribute administration
nodes.full: As a satrapal land, Maka owed the Persian king an annual render — the reliefs show camels and cloth — and provided troops. It is the first time the peninsula's oases were folded into an imperial fiscal system.
nodes.src: Achaemenid tribute lists (Herodotus 3.93 groups Maka with the 14th nome); the Maciya gift-bearers at Persepolis.

nodes.label: The Iron Age snake shrines
nodes.full: At springs and hilltop shrines across the peninsula, Iron Age communities deposited bronze and clay snakes, snake-decorated bowls and incense burners. The serpent — guardian of water and the underworld — is the clearest religious symbol the period has left.
nodes.src: A. Benoist, 'The Iron Age snake cult in the Oman peninsula' (2016); Masafi and Bithnah shrine excavations (French mission); Saruq al-Hadid snake objects (Dubai).

nodes.label: The mudbrick shrines of Masafi and Bithnah
nodes.full: Distinct from the portable snake objects, the Iron Age left purpose-built cult buildings — small mudbrick rooms with benches, altars and pillared porticos at Masafi and Bithnah, set by springs or on low hills. They are the peninsula's first free-standing temples.
nodes.src: A. Benoist et al. on the Masafi-3 and Bithnah-44 cult buildings (French archaeological mission in the UAE); the distinction between shrine architecture and the snake-object assemblage.

nodes.label: Incense and the altar
nodes.full: Cuboid stone incense burners, some carved with architectural or animal motifs, appear across Iron Age shrines and halls — evidence that aromatic burning, the ritual that would define Arabian religion for the next millennium, was already central here.
nodes.src: Iron Age III South Arabian-style incense burners at Muweilah and Rumeilah (Magee; Boucharlat & Lombard); the link to the emerging incense trade.

nodes.label: The gold and iron of Saruq al-Hadid
nodes.full: A dune site deep in the desert yielded thousands of Iron Age objects — gold rings and beads, bronze arrowheads, snake figurines, iron slag — around what seems to have been a seasonal metalworking and ritual gathering place. One gold ring is now the emblem of the Emirate of Dubai.
nodes.src: Saruq al-Hadid excavations (Dubai Municipality; German and Spanish teams); the site's gold assemblage in the Saruq Al-Hadid Archaeology Museum.

nodes.label: An Iron Age copper-alloy vessel with rattles
nodes.full: Iron Age shrine and settlement assemblages include small bells, pellet-rattles and bridge-spouted vessels used in libation. These are the peninsula's earliest sound-making objects, tied to the snake-shrine ritual rather than to entertainment.
nodes.src: Rattle and bell finds from Iron Age contexts noted by Benoist (2016) and in the Bithnah and Rumeilah reports; interpretation as ritual sound instruments.

nodes.label: The surveying knowledge behind the falaj
nodes.full: To run water for kilometres through a tunnel on a gradient of a few metres per kilometre — steep enough to flow, gentle enough not to erode — required accurate levelling and an understanding of the water table. This applied hydraulics is the peninsula's great Iron Age intellectual achievement.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti (2002) on falaj construction technique; comparison with the qanat tradition of the Iranian plateau (debate on direction of transmission).

nodes.label: The oral order under Persian rule
nodes.full: Even folded into the Achaemenid Empire, whose administration ran on written Aramaic, the Maka oases kept their accounting, water shares and genealogy in memory and social practice. Indigenous writing does not appear until the Hellenistic age at Mleiha — a persistent oral order, not a lag.
nodes.src: The near-absence of indigenous inscriptions in south-east Arabia before c.300 BC (Cleuziou & Tosi 2007/2020); the first local scripts at Mleiha (Hasaitic / Aramaic) in the following period.

nodes.label: The falaj revolution and the Iron Age harvest
nodes.full: By tapping groundwater and carrying it to land that rain never reached, the falaj roughly multiplied the area that could be farmed. Date and cereal output rose, and with it population — the Iron Age is the peninsula's first demographic boom.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti (2002); Magee on Iron Age settlement density; palaeobotanical evidence for expanded cereal and date cultivation.

nodes.label: Domestication of the dromedary camel
nodes.full: The earliest secure evidence for domestic dromedaries — dung, penned animals, gnawed bones — comes from south-east Arabian Iron Age sites around 1000 BC. The pack camel gave the peninsula's people a way to cross the deserts that had always hemmed them in.
nodes.src: P. Magee, 'When was the dromedary domesticated in the ancient Near East?', ZOrA 8 (2015); the Muweilah camel evidence.

nodes.label: The falaj / qanat water tunnel
nodes.full: A mother-well sunk to the aquifer, a gently graded tunnel, and a line of vertical shafts for air and spoil removal — the falaj is one of the earliest large-scale groundwater technologies anywhere, and south-east Arabia has a claim to inventing it.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti, PSAS 32 (2002); the Iron Age aflaj at al-Ain are part of the UNESCO 'Cultural Sites of Al Ain' inscription (2011).

nodes.label: Iron working reaches the peninsula
nodes.full: Iron slag, blooms and finished tools at Saruq al-Hadid — the site's name means 'the way of iron' — and other Iron Age settlements show the new metal being smelted and forged alongside the older bronze. The peninsula adopted iron in step with the wider Near East.
nodes.src: Iron-working debris at Saruq al-Hadid (Dubai Municipality excavations) and Iron Age sites; the regional Iron Age metallurgy in Magee, 'The Archaeology of Prehistoric Arabia' (2014).

nodes.label: The camel opens the overland route to south Arabia
nodes.full: Once the dromedary was domesticated, Magan's oases were no longer islands. Caravans could now cross to south Arabia, tying the peninsula into the incense trade and the overland networks that would define the next thousand years.
nodes.src: Magee (2015) on the domestication date; the subsequent integration of south-east Arabia into peninsular caravan trade (Iron Age III incense burners at Muweilah, Rumeilah).

nodes.label: Maka among the lands of the Great King
nodes.full: On the Apadana staircase at Persepolis, the delegation of Maciya — the Oman peninsula — brings a dromedary and folded garments to Darius. Magan's relationship with the wider world is now that of a subject province bringing gifts to court.
nodes.src: The Maciya delegation, Apadana east stairs, Persepolis; Achaemenid land-lists (DNa, DSe). Schmidt, 'Persepolis' (1953).

nodes.label: The Achaemenid Empire annexes Maka
nodes.full: Under Cyrus and Cambyses the Persian Empire absorbed the Oman peninsula as the satrapal land of Maka, giving it — for the first time — a formal place in a state that stretched from the Aegean to the Indus.
nodes.src: Maka in the Bisitun inscription (already a subject land under Darius, 522 BC), implying annexation under Cyrus/Cambyses; Herodotus 3.93.

nodes.label: The pack camel as a transport revolution
nodes.full: Camel domestication in south-east Arabia is part of a peninsula-wide shift: within a few centuries, caravans reshaped Arabian trade, warfare and settlement. The Oman peninsula was at or near the origin of a change that made the deep desert crossable.
nodes.src: Magee (2015); the broader Arabian camel-domestication debate (Uerpmann & Uerpmann; Heide).

nodes.label: Weapons in Iron Age women's graves
nodes.full: Some Iron Age burials in the peninsula pair adult women with bronze arrowheads and blades. Whether these mark hunters, fighters or symbolic status, they complicate any simple assumption that weapons meant men.
nodes.src: Spanish mission reports on al-Thuqaibah / Wadi al-Qawr Iron Age cemeteries; the association of weapons with sexed female skeletons noted but debated.

nodes.label: The oasis-village household
nodes.full: Iron Age houses — mudbrick rooms around courtyards, with storage jars, grinding stones and hearths — cluster along the falaj channels. The household that held a timed share of the water was the basic unit of the new agricultural society, and the one the falaj rota was written around.
nodes.src: Domestic architecture at Rumeilah (Boucharlat & Lombard), al-Thuqaibah (Spanish mission) and Salut (Italian mission); the falaj-shareholding household as the social unit (Cleuziou & Tosi 2007/2020).
